content: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS) typically occurs without any preceding symptoms, making it a sudden and unexpected event. Infants who succumb to SIDS are often asymptomatic prior to the event. The condition is generally used to describe all unexpected deaths in infants. History and Symptoms Most infants affected by SIDS do not exhibit any noticeable symptoms before the event. History In some cases, a detailed history may reveal certain factors or observations, including: Infants who were placed in a prone sleeping position (on their stomach) immediately after feeding. Parents may report that routine checks during the infant's sleep were unremarkable, but the infant was later found deceased. Some parents may describe their infant as not being themselves in the hours leading up to the event. A history of symptoms such as diarrhea, vomiting, or fatigue occurring up to two weeks prior to the infant's death may be reported by some parents. A history of apnea (temporary cessation of breathing) may be present in some infants. Swallowing dysfunction may also be noted in some cases. A thorough evaluation for potential child abuse should always be considered. Brainstem anomalies may be identified in some infants. Genetic mutations or cardiac ion channel defects may be present. Questions for Parents Physicians should ask parents specific questions to gather a comprehensive history regarding the infant, including: 1. Was there any trauma to the infant? 2. Did the infant ingest any foreign objects? 3. Is there a history of apnea? If so, inquire about the duration of apnea episodes in seconds. 4. Were there any incidents prior to the Brief Resolved Unexplained Event (BRUE)? 5. Were there any signs of paroxysmal coughing? 6. Were there any symptoms of an upper respiratory tract infection? 7. Did the infant exhibit symptoms of gastroesophageal reflux (GER) after feeding? 8. What was the time and amount of the infant's last meal? 9. What position was the infant placed in when put to sleep? 10. Was there any change in the infant's color? If so, ask the parent to describe the color change. If the parent mentions a blue discoloration, ask how pronounced the blue color was. 11. Was there any specific event? If so, inquire about the duration of the event. 12. What was the infant's body tone during the event? For example, was the baby stiff or shaking? 13. Did the parents perform CPR after the incident? If so, ask them to describe how it was performed. These detailed questions and observations are critical for understanding the circumstances surrounding the event and for ruling out other potential causes of death.
